name: Decision Tree Classifier
analogy: Think of it as a checklist a cautious trader runs before every entry. Each line is a yes-or-no question about the bar, the answers lead down one path, and where the path ends is a note saying how often past bars like this one went on to hit the profit target.

steps.title: Label every training bar with what happened
steps.description: Each training bar is tagged with its real outcome, for example which of the profit target or the stop was touched first. The tree learns only from these tags.
steps.inExample: Out of 30,000 bars, 51 percent touched the 20-point profit target first and 49 percent touched the 20-point stop first.

steps.title: Decide whether rare outcomes need extra weight
steps.description: Because splits chase overall purity, a rare outcome can get lost. If one outcome is much rarer than the other, its bars are given extra weight so the tree pays attention to them; if the outcomes are balanced, nothing is changed.
steps.inExample: Target-first and stop-first are close to balanced here, so no extra weight is applied.

steps.title: Find the question that unmixes the outcomes best
steps.description: The model tries many yes-or-no questions on every feature and scores how much more one-sided the outcomes become on each side. The question that purifies the groups most is chosen for the top of the tree.
steps.inExample: 'Is the relative strength index under 35?' wins: the yes side is 54 percent target-first, the no side 50 percent.

steps.title: Split and repeat down each branch
steps.description: Each side of the split gets its own best question, and so on down. A branch asks only about the bars that reached it, so deep questions can be very specific.
steps.inExample: On the oversold branch the next question is 'is the close more than one and a half standard deviations below its 20-bar average?', then 'is volume more than 30 percent above normal?'.

steps.title: Stop at a sensible depth
steps.description: The tree is told when to stop: a maximum depth or a minimum number of bars in a leaf. Without limits it would memorize the training bars, so the limit is the main protection against overfitting.
steps.inExample: Depth is capped at 4 questions and every leaf must hold at least 100 bars.

steps.title: Store the outcome mix in every leaf
steps.description: Each leaf remembers the share of each outcome among the training bars that ended there. That share, not just a yes or no, is what the model reports as its probability.
steps.inExample: One leaf holds 143 bars of which 80 were target-first, so it stores 56 percent target-first and 44 percent stop-first.

steps.title: Walk a new bar down the tree
steps.description: A new bar answers each question in turn, follows one path to a leaf, and receives that leaf's stored outcome mix as its answer. The path itself is the explanation.
steps.inExample: The new bar answers yes, yes, yes, yes, lands in the 143-bar leaf and is scored 56 percent target-first.

useFor.example: Scoring each long entry on MNQ 5-minute bars as 'target first' or 'stop first' and showing the exact path that produced the score.

useFor.task: Classifying the outcome of a trade setup
useFor.example: Predicting which of a 20-point target, a 20-point stop or a 12-bar time limit is reached first, using the 35 base features.
Reading how often relative strength index and volume ratio are used near the top of the tree to decide which of the 151 indicators to keep.

useFor.task: A shallow building block for ensembles
useFor.example: Using trees only 2 or 3 questions deep as the small pieces inside a boosted model.

avoidWhen: You want the most accurate probabilities; one tree gives coarse, step-like probabilities and is easily shaken by small data changes, while a forest or boosted model smooths this out.
The target is a rare event such as a large move in 2 percent of bars and you have not re-weighted; the tree may simply call every bar the common class.

example.scenario: A 5-minute MNQ bar closes after a sharp drop. A trader is considering a long entry with a 20-point target and a 20-point stop, and asks the tree which is more likely to be reached first.

input.summary: One row of features describing the bar that just closed, plus the shape of the trade being considered.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 5-minute bar closed.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; under 30 is commonly read as oversold.

fields.name: distance below the 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How stretched the close is below its recent average, scaled by recent variation.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading in this bar was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

fields.name: trade being considered
fields.meaning: The two levels whose order of arrival the tree is asked about; one point on MNQ is worth 2 US dollars.

output.summary: The outcome mix of the leaf the bar landed in, and the path that got it there.

fields.name: probability the target is hit first
fields.meaning: The share of training bars in this leaf whose 20-point target was reached before the 20-point stop.

fields.name: probability the stop is hit first
fields.meaning: The remaining share of training bars in this leaf.

fields.name: bars in the leaf
fields.meaning: How many past bars the probabilities are based on.

fields.name: path
fields.value: index under 35, stretch beyond one and a half standard deviations, volume over 30 percent above normal, range under 30
fields.meaning: The four answers that led to this leaf.

example.reading: With a target and stop of equal size, 56 percent target-first is a modest lean of six points over a coin flip, and whether it pays depends on costs and on whether the leaf's share holds on bars the tree has not seen. Check it on later walk-forward folds before trading it.
